source.title: Shared Representational Geometry Across Neural Networks
source.authors: Qihong Lu; Po-Hsuan Chen; J. Pillow; P. Ramadge; K. Norman; U. Hasson

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests convergence across independently trained networks using SRM orthogonal alignment and RSM comparisons, rather than the original sources’ methods.
record.gate_note: Tests same-architecture networks trained on CIFAR10/CIFAR100, including how their measured alignment changes during training. It does not test model scaling, cross-modal alignment, or unrelated architectures trained on different objectives or data. Figure 3 results described only qualitatively in the supplied text are recorded as such; no values are inferred from the missing plots.
record.test_reason: It trains 10 same-architecture networks per setting (ConvNets and ResNet18 on CIFAR10/100) from different initializations. It then asks whether an orthogonal SRM map aligns them into a shared space. This is the convergent-learning question (V3) and a linear-mappability question (V4), answered with a different method from Li et al.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that different same-architecture networks trained on the same data encode inputs as different orthogonal transformations of a shared representation, so their representational geometry is the same. This holds especially well for ConvNets and somewhat less for ResNet18 and early layers. They suggest higher-capacity models may learn qualitatively different representations, and attribute the sharing to common inputs and objective, without testing that attribution.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SRM to find orthogonal transformations and compares inter-network with within-network RSMs; experiments are on same-dataset ConvNets and ResNet18 rather than testing scale or cross-modal alignment.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment varies by layer and architecture: it is weaker in early ConvNet layers and ResNet18 than in ConvNet final layers. The paper also reports differences across CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 final-layer variance explained.

fits_no_version.finding: Across seeds, the higher-capacity ResNet18 aligns less well than small ConvNets. The authors suggest high-capacity models may learn qualitatively different representations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within one architecture family, cross-seed alignment may decrease with model capacity. This is opposite in direction to V1's scale trend, but tested only same-architecture and confounded with architecture.

record.peer_reviewed: 32nd Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2018)
record.problems: Experiments use networks trained on the same datasets and classification objective, and do not establish whether shared data/objectives cause the alignment. The tested architecture and task range is limited. Several Figure 3 outcomes are described qualitatively in the supplied text without numerical values.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep. No different architectures, objectives or data.
No vision-language or paired image-caption models.
No interpretable feature or unit matching; the study uses only subspace/geometry alignment.
Only orthogonal SRM maps between same-architecture networks. No stitching, relative representations, unpaired mapping, or task-performance loss after mapping.
No interpretable neurons, SAE features or circuits.
No comparison of similarity measures, settings, or out-of-distribution inputs. Only a remark that linear and rank correlation gave similar results in the simulation.
No cross-model convergence test and no plateau test. The shared input/objective explanation is asserted in the Discussion, not tested.

missing.what: Layer-wise SRM variance explained for each ConvNet and ResNet18 layer, including ResNet18 CIFAR100 values
Shared-space RSM correlation values at the end of training, per layer and model
Between-network within-RSM correlation values per layer and model

record.verdict_notes: Removed the V7 links and the V7 label. The study compares only same-architecture seed replicates, and its causal explanation is speculation in the Discussion. r6 is a method check on synthetic transforms. Most per-layer results are figure-only; only the 91%/89% figures are stated in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over model size or capability, and no test of alignment across different architectures, objectives, or data.
No vision-language models or paired image-caption representations.
Tests representational geometry across trained networks and orthogonal shared spaces, but does not test recurrence of interpretable features or whether individual units are shared.
Tests SRM orthogonal transformations between activity patterns; does not test stitching, relative representations, or mapping without paired data.
No interpretable neurons, SAE features, or circuits are identified or compared.
Uses RSM and tests CIFAR10/CIFAR100, but does not compare reasonable similarity measures or test out-of-distribution inputs or sensitivity to similarity settings.

Reports incomplete alignment in some layers/networks and proposes shared input/objective as an explanation, but does not causally vary data or objectives, compare against a common-reality account, or test for a plateau.

rows.subject: Trained neural network on a toy classification task
rows.stage_stated: trained on a toy classification task
rows.operation_detail: Multiplied hidden activity patterns by ten random orthogonal (or permutation) matrices, fit SRM on an alignment set, and assessed alignment on held-out test patterns.
rows.measure: Correlation between average inter-network RSM and average within-network RSM
rows.value: Shared-space inter-network RSM is highly similar to the average within-network RSM; exact values not stated in text
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrapped confidence interval based on 50 simulation runs; numeric interval not stated
rows.locator: Results; Figure 2 and Simulation: SRM can identify orthogonal transformations
rows.note: This is a synthetic alignment validation, not evidence that naturally trained networks independently acquire the imposed transformations.
rows.check: This is a method-validation simulation. The orthogonal transforms were imposed artificially on one network's activity, so it shows SRM can recover a known transform. It is not evidence that independently trained models are interchangeable, so it should not count toward V4.

rows.subject: ConvNets (10 networks; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared native-space inter-network RSM with within-network RSM before SRM alignment.
rows.measure: Similarity of inter-network and within-network RSMs
rows.value: Native-space inter-network RSM is dissimilar from within-network RSM
rows.note: The paper attributes the lack of similarity to misalignment; SRM alignment is assessed separately.
rows.check: Recorded as 'absent' against a within-network baseline. Read correctly, native-space misalignment shows different networks do not share the same basis or units. V3 says exactly this ('not the same individual units or bases'), so the row is consistent with V3 rather than an absent effect. It is a qualitative figure observation with no number, and has no bearing on V4 on its own.
